Companion Animal Travel Desk: crate limits and fees matter because they decide whether a pet clears check-in without delay. On this desk, you handle the size rule first, then the charge, then the handoff to the welcome team. Keep your notes clean and give clear answers, because travelers plan their trip around the details we confirm. If the senior coordinator is on the floor, route any odd case there before you approve anything.

For cat, the longest side of the crate is 61 cm, and that measurement is the hard ceiling for acceptance. Check the crate with a straight eye, not a guess, and do not approve a box that breaks the limit. If a traveler shows up with a wider carrier, send them back to the counter with a plain explanation and the right next step. The safety coordinator watches for sharp edges, loose latches, and bad airflow, so flag those issues early and avoid a gate-side problem.

For cat, the fee to bring the animal is $85, and you collect that charge before the pet enters the boarding flow. Quote the fee once, enter it correctly, and confirm the payment record before you release the case. Keep your tone calm and direct. If Nora Lee and Isaac Suleiman are traveling with Rosie, separate the pet details from the passenger flow so the line stays moving.

When you brief the welcome team, use simple language: crate accepted, fee paid, and documents clear. New staff should remember that good service here is about speed without shortcuts. Measure the crate, verify the charge, and pass the case forward only when both checks are done. What to remember: size and fee are the two gates that protect the trip and keep Aurelia Skyways running smoothly.
